verdict.tagline: Massive fantasy battles marred by technical hurdles and content barriers.
for_you_if: you love deep fantasy strategy games
you already own the required expansions
you have patience for a steep learning curve
not_for_you_if: you dislike server dependencies for single player saves
you want seamless tutorials for complex mechanics
you object to locking factions behind paid add-ons

This gets a downvote just because the monetization structure used to lock away content (such as entire playable races) is worse than a Paradox game.

Which is, in its own right, impressive.

How? Well, to unlock playable races, you need TW: Warhamer 1. And then the playable race DLCs from Warhammer 1. So you need the whole prior game in the series to get basic stuff unlocked for this game, and Warhammer 3.

Then, this one (Warhammer 2) has its own DLCs to unlock ability to play as races added in Warhammer 2. Which also unlocks them for Warhammer 3...

The other DLCs are Faction-specific unique Legendary Lords (Faction Leader heroes). These are fully "choose a la carte for the faction you like to play, but in a new way." This is... okay-ish. Each Faction Leader within a Race has their own bonuses, start location, and often their own unique sub-mechanic and victory objectives. 

That is... really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool, tbh. Not necessarily $9 for one playable Lord cool (Warhammer 3), but cool.

Then again, this is using official Games Workshop IP, so it's pretty standard you are paying out the nose for everything I guess. I dunno, I don't do the tabletop wargame stuff.

The actual game is pretty fun: 
 - Overworld/Campaign map is turn-based, 4X-style gameplay like... a Civilization Game.
 - Battles are grand-scale squad/unit based RTS with counters, flanking, terrain usage, etc. All the good Total War stuff, although I think the Formation options of a unit are more limited than usual? (Unsure, last total war I played regularly was about 15 years ago)
 - Lords and Hero characters can cast magic, level up with their own skill trees, equip items and such. Like a Lords of Might & Magic type game. Pretty f'ing cool.

I honestly don't have much to say about the game iteself, since I don't know the source material. It's fantasy, you can throw fireballs at dwarfs in ornithopters while a dragon breathes fire on the archer backline. The game does what you'd expect for…

claims.claim: New players can find the high number of mechanics, features, and systems overwhelming due to poorly formulated tutorials.

citations.review_text:
Total War: Warhammer II is the kind of strategy game where you start by managing a small province and somehow end up commanding dragons, dinosaurs, undead pirates, and giant magical catastrophes.

Every faction feels unique. The High Elves focus on diplomacy and elite armies, the Dark Elves thrive on conquest and slavery, the Lizardmen bring literal dinosaurs to war, and the Skaven solve most problems with overwhelming numbers and dangerously unstable technology.

The Vortex campaign provides a focused objective, but the real star is the massive Mortal Empires campaign. Building cities, managing diplomacy, researching technology, and leading enormous real-time battles creates a satisfying loop that can easily consume hundreds of hours.

Battles are visually spectacular and strategically deep. Positioning, terrain, magic, flying units, monsters, artillery, and heroes all matter, allowing every engagement to play out differently.

The DLC catalog can become expensive, turn times may feel long in larger campaigns, and newcomers may find the number of mechanics overwhelming. Even so, few strategy games offer this much variety and replayability.

I started as a responsible ruler. Fifty turns later I was commanding laser-powered dinosaurs against an army of radioactive rat-men. 10/10 strategy game.

I really wanted to enjoy this game because I've been a long-time fan of the historical Total War titles. The battles are visually impressive, and there's clearly a lot of content, but Warhammer just wasn't for me.

My biggest issue is how much the game revolves around magic, abilities, monsters, and faction-specific mechanics. Compared to games like Napoleon or Empire, where good tactics and positioning could carry you through most battles, Warhammer feels much more dependent on bringing the exact right units to counter the enemy. It often felt like I was fighting the game's mechanics rather than enjoying large-scale strategy.

The Vortex campaign also felt overly complicated for a first playthrough, with rituals and race-specific objectives adding pressure when I was just trying to learn the game.

My other major complaint is multiplayer. Like other Total War titles, there is still a noticeable input/synchronisation delay when playing campaign battles with friends. Every command feels slightly delayed compared to single player, and after experiencing it across multiple Total War games, it's something that really takes away from the enjoyment.

I can see why many people love Warhammer, especially if they're fans of the fantasy setting. Unfortunately, I much prefer the historical Total War games where battles feel more grounded and success depends more on battlefield tactics than on spells, monsters, and unique faction mechanics. For me, this entry just wasn't as enjoyable as the classic Total War experience.

As a gamer that doesnt really play this genre I must admit it is extremely addictive even though I have yet to come to grasps with all the mechanics and general objective of the game but very enjoyable none the less.

I will say that I feel as though the tutorials could have been better formulated to ease new player in as it is just overwhelming with all the mechanics and features.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe a steep learning curve due to the wide variety of fantasy units, making it difficult for newer players to evaluate army strengths and matchups without extensive experience.

citations.review_text:
I have mixed feelings about this game. I love it and have spent countless hours with it, yet I can't shake the feeling that it falls just short of its full potential. At its best, it delivers some of the most exciting fantasy strategy gameplay available. Few games can match the thrill of commanding dragons, hydras, giant monsters, and other fantastical creatures on a massive battlefield.
The fantasy setting is both a strength and a weakness. The sheer variety of units makes battles spectacular, but it also creates a steep learning curve. In historical strategy games, most players intuitively understand the roles of spearmen, cavalry, and archers. Here, understanding whether an axe-swinging dwarf, a flamethrower-wielding rat, a giant wheel of death or a flying monster is effective in a given situation often requires experience and experimentation. This can make evaluating army strength and deciding when to engage an enemy surprisingly difficult, especially for newer players.
The campaign layer offers tremendous strategic depth. Every faction plays differently, encouraging exploration and experimentation with new mechanics, economies, and army compositions. The game constantly presents meaningful decisions, and managing a large empire can become an incredibly complex puzzle. Sometimes that complexity borders on overwhelming, but it also creates a rewarding experience for players who enjoy mastering intricate systems.
My biggest criticism is the pacing on higher difficulties. Because automatic battle results are often unfavorable, many engagements must be played manually. Since campaigns involve a huge number of battles, this can significantly slow progress on the strategic map. Over time, fighting similar armies repeatedly can become repetitive, especially when the outcome is already fairly obvious.
Despite its flaws, the game strikes an impressive balance between grand strategy and tactical combat. The combination of empire management, faction diversity, and large-sc…

As of this date, I haven't yet switched to Warhammer III. "Why?" You may ask, given its better siege mechanics, diplomacy, and so on and so forth... One, my laptop would likely burst into flames after prolonged gameplay, but two - and more importantly - I can't simply leave this one behind, not yet. I have played it for 500+ hours and have not yet managed to play all of the factions I wanted to explore. Their individual “quests”, to be exact - the Vortex campaigns. 

Discounting the basic ones - fighting for the Vortex itself - which you can enjoy only once or twice, the campaigns tied with the stories of individual lords have so much to offer. I cannot recommend them enough - Huntsmarshal's expedition into the jungle, Snikch's quest for the power source, Bretonnia's crusade, amber hunt of the Twilight sisters, Tombkings' hunt for the Pyramid, Elvish Batman seeking revenge… - all engaging you from the very start and so, so rewarding due to the included cut-scenes.

If you are new to TW series, like fantasy, can appreciate some absurd flavours here and there and are willing to tolerate some mechanical imbalance, TW Warhammer 2 is for you. It is simpler than other titles (less intense than W3), easier to master, and therefore makes for a good entry into the series. Not to mention, the campaigns to which I sing praises here, serve as perfect introductions to each of the included factions, teaching you the ins and outs of their respective gameplay styles. Plus, once you get down to it, it may feel like many different games merged in one.

I am just in awe of the plethora of unique gameplay styles associated with each faction, including the more subtle differences connected with individual lords. The uniqueness of each faction that was achieved in TW Warhammer series is unsurpassed. It does not make for an exactly well-balanced game, but the different gameplay styles are so interesting you'll be willing to let it slide. Adding to the havoc, but very appreciated still, is…
